intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive dilated cardiomyopathy-2A (CMD2A) is caused by homozygous mutation in the gene encoding cardiac troponin I (TNNI3). Heterozygous mutations in TNNI3 have also been reported in families with autosomal dominant dilated cardiomyopathy.

checks.claim: Autosomal recessive dilated cardiomyopathy-2A (CMD2A) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TNNI3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified a novel TNNI3 mutation in a family with recessive disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a recessive TNNI3 mutation, and its closing line about 'mutation analyses designed to identify homozygous mutations' points to homozygosity. But it never says outright that the patients were homozygous, and it doesn't use the name CMD2A.

checks.explanation: The abstract identifies TNNI3 as the gene for cardiac troponin I.

checks.claim: Heterozygous mutations in TNNI3 have been reported in families with autosomal dominant dilated cardiomyopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: These are the first reported autosomal dominant DCM-causing mutations in TNNI3
checks.explanation: The abstract reports autosomal dominant DCM mutations in families but never says the carriers were heterozygous. Heterozygosity is implied by dominant inheritance, not stated.

paragraphs.text: Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy is a common cause of heart failure (Murphy et al., 2004). Familial isolated dilated cardiomyopathy is usually reported as autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and expressivity, but an autosomal recessive form has also been described (Goldblatt et al., 1987). In a study of infants of Arab descent, Seliem et al. (2000) found that onset was usually before 30 months of age and mortality was high.

paragraphs.text: Seliem et al. (2000) studied 55 consecutive patients younger than 10 years of age with dilated cardiomyopathy, seen over a 5-year period in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia. Echocardiography was the primary diagnostic method. The 55 patients came from 41 families of Arab descent and made up 20% of the offspring in those families. In 19 families (46%) the parents were first cousins; the other 22 families (54%) had no obvious consanguinity. Of the patients, 95% presented before 30 months of age (range, 1 to 100 months). Females made up 62% of patients and males 38%. Of the patients, 25 (46%) died, 15 (27%) improved, and 15 (27%) recovered. Left ventricular shortening fraction at diagnosis ranged from 5 to 28% and did not differ among those who died, improved, or recovered.

paragraphs.text: Murphy et al. (2004) analyzed the TNNI3 gene, which encodes cardiac troponin I, in 235 patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. They used a method able to detect both dominant and recessive mutations. They found a novel TNNI3 mutation in a family with recessive disease. Functional studies showed impaired troponin interactions, which could reduce myocardial contractility. Murphy et al. (2004) stated that TNNI3 was the first gene identified for recessive dilated cardiomyopathy.

paragraphs.text: Carballo et al. (2009) screened TNNI3 exons by heteroduplex analysis in 96 probands with dilated cardiomyopathy, then sequenced exons with abnormal profiles. They identified 2 novel missense mutations, lys36-to-gln (K36Q) and asn185-to-lys (N185K). Each was associated with severe, early-onset familial dilated cardiomyopathy. Variants were evaluated by segregation analysis and by study of normal controls. Of the 5 mutation carriers, 3 needed cardiac transplantation, at ages 6, 15, and 24 years. Troponin reconstituted with either mutant troponin I gave a lower maximum actin-tropomyosin-activated myosin ATPase rate and lower calcium sensitivity than wildtype. Mutant thin filaments also had reduced calcium affinity. Carballo et al. (2009) stated that these were the first reported autosomal dominant mutations in TNNI3 causing dilated cardiomyopathy.
